title: The method that forgot its fleet

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where the demo opens the dock: one scan out, the free boat list, one scan in.

tasks.title: Catch the methods losing their fleet
tasks.description:
Before you change anything, capture both crashes. In `src/reproduce.js`, implement `reproduceLostThis()`.

With the original `Fleet`, make a fleet of `['K1', 'K2', 'P1']`, then:

- call `fleet.freeBoats()` and keep the `message` of the error it throws
- make a scanner with `createScanner()`, wire it with `connectScanner(scanner, fleet)`, call `scanner.scan('out', 'K1')` and keep that error's `message`

Return `{ freeBoatsError, scannerError }`, both strings. The check runs your function against the original `fleet.js`.
nextSteps: Run `node src/demo.js` and read the three errors.
Wrap each call in its own `try...catch`.
Keep `err.message` from each and return both.
Read the messages and ask which object was undefined.
hints: Both calls throw a TypeError. Return the messages, not the error objects, so they survive being printed as JSON.
A small helper that runs a function and returns the message of whatever it throws keeps this short.
Both messages say that something is undefined while reading `out`. That something is `this`.

tasks.title: Methods that remember their fleet
tasks.description:
Fix `Fleet` in `src/fleet.js` so its methods work wherever they are called from.

- `checkOut(id)`, `checkIn(id)` and `isFree(id)` keep working when taken off the fleet and called as plain functions, such as `boatIds.filter(fleet.isFree)`, `const { checkIn } = fleet` or a scanner handler.
- Each method stays tied to the fleet it came from. Two fleets never share boats.
- `freeBoats()` returns the ids of boats that are not out, in fleet order.
- `checkOut` of a boat that is already out still throws an error that says `already out`.

Leave `dock.js` unchanged: the check uses the original one.
nextSteps: Find every place a Fleet method is handed to other code.
Pick one way to tie the methods to their fleet for good.
Make sure it is done per fleet, not once for the class.
Run `node src/demo.js` and check all three steps.
hints: `this` is decided by how a function is called, not where it was written. `fleet.isFree(id)` sets it, `isFree(id)` does not.
Fixing the call inside `freeBoats` only fixes that one caller. The scanner in `dock.js` calls the methods as plain functions too.
Arrow functions take `this` from where they are created. A class field like `isFree = (id) => ...` creates one per fleet, tied to it. Binding each method in the constructor also works.

tasks.title: Write the test that would have caught it
tasks.description:
Write vitest tests in `src/fleet.test.js` that use `Fleet` the way Cinderbay does:

- `freeBoats()` after a boat is checked out
- `checkOut` and `checkIn` through a scanner from `dock.js`, wired with `connectScanner`

The check runs your test file three times: beside the original `fleet.js` (it must fail), beside a correct fix (it must pass) and beside a fix that only repairs the call inside `freeBoats` (it must fail).
nextSteps: Write a test that checks a boat out and asserts `freeBoats()`.
Write a test that wires a scanner and scans a boat out and in.
Assert the free boats after each scan.
hints: A test that only calls methods as `fleet.method()` will never see this bug. Use the methods the way other code does.
Import `createScanner` and `connectScanner` from `dock.js`. The real wiring is the best test of it.
The freeBoats only fix passes your first test. Only the scanner test fails beside it, because `checkOut` still loses `this`.
